title: KFC
subtitle: Rebuilding the path from menu to checkout
summary: Redesigned the ordering flows for one of the largest QSR brands in the region, shortening the distance between a hungry customer and a placed order.
context: KFC customers were dropping out between the menu and the payment screen. The flow had grown by accretion — new deal types, new delivery modes and new payment methods had each been bolted onto a structure that was never designed to hold them.
challenge: Reduce the number of decisions between opening the app and confirming an order, without removing the deals and customisation that drive basket size.

approach.title: Mapped the existing order journey end to end
approach.body: Walked the live flow on every platform and mode — delivery, pickup, dine-in — and marked every screen where the customer had to make a decision, wait, or go back.

approach.title: Separated choosing from configuring
approach.body: Browsing the menu and configuring an item were competing for the same screen. Splitting them let the menu stay fast to scan while customisation got the room it needed.

approach.title: Moved mode and address selection up front
approach.body: Delivery mode, store and address were being confirmed late, which invalidated menu availability. Resolving them first meant the menu a customer saw was the menu they could actually order from.

approach.title: Rebuilt the cart as a review step, not a detour
approach.body: Deals, upsells and applied offers were consolidated into one reviewable summary so the final confirmation carried no surprises.

approach.title: Tested and iterated with real users
approach.body: Ran moderated usability sessions on the prototype, watched where people hesitated, and reworked the steps that produced the pauses.

outcomes: A shorter, more predictable route from menu to checkout
Customisation and deals preserved rather than stripped out
Flows documented and handed to development with open questions already settled
Patterns reused across sibling brands in the same portfolio
contributions: End-to-end UX for the ordering journey
UI design on the client design system

title: KFC UAE
subtitle: A performance dashboard for the people running the market
summary: A performance dashboard built on the client’s own design system, giving the market team one place to read how stores, channels and campaigns were actually doing.
context: Performance data lived in several places and each team read it differently. Answering a straightforward question — how did this campaign do in this city — meant assembling it by hand.
challenge: Design a dashboard that answers the questions the team asks most, first, and stays legible as the number of tracked metrics grows.

approach.title: Started from the questions, not the metrics
approach.body: Interviewed the people who would use it daily and wrote down the questions they actually asked. The layout follows that order of enquiry rather than the shape of the database.

approach.title: Set a hierarchy: headline, then breakdown, then detail
approach.body: The top of the screen answers "is anything wrong". Everything below it exists to answer "where" and "why", in that order.

approach.title: Worked inside the client design system
approach.body: Every component came from the client library. Where a chart pattern did not exist, I proposed it in their token vocabulary so it could be adopted rather than sit as an exception.

approach.title: Designed the empty, loading and partial states
approach.body: Dashboards spend real time in states that are not "all data loaded". Each one was specified so the build did not have to improvise.

outcomes: A single screen the market team could open to answer their standing questions
Chart and table patterns contributed back to the client design system
Complete state coverage, so nothing was invented at build time
contributions: Data visualisation patterns within the client system

title: Hero FinCorp
subtitle: Personal finance management, prototyped end to end
summary: Interactive personal finance management prototypes built on the client’s design system — money in, money out, and the decisions in between made legible.
context: Personal finance features tend to be judged on whether someone can look at a screen and immediately understand their own position. Static mockups could not settle that question, so the work was prototyped.
challenge: Turn transaction data into something a person can read in a glance and act on — spending, categories, and trends — without the interface reading as a spreadsheet.

approach.title: Built a category model people recognise
approach.body: Categories only work if they match how someone already thinks about their spending. The taxonomy was drafted, tested against real statements, and cut down until it stopped needing explanation.

approach.title: Designed for the glance and the dig
approach.body: A summary anyone can read in two seconds, with progressive detail behind it for the person who wants to know exactly where a number came from.

approach.title: Prototyped the motion, not just the screens
approach.body: Interactive prototypes let stakeholders feel the transitions between summary and detail — the part of the experience a flat comp cannot communicate.

approach.title: Stayed inside the client design system
approach.body: Everything was assembled from existing components so the prototype doubled as a buildable specification.

outcomes: Clickable prototypes used to align stakeholders before build
A spending taxonomy that held up against real statement data
Interaction and motion decisions settled ahead of development
contributions: UX for the PFM feature set
UI design within the client design system

title: Three-Tier Token System
subtitle: The design system that cut the design–dev back-and-forth
summary: A three-tier token architecture — primitive, semantic, component — now used across product teams, built to end the recurring argument about which grey this grey is.
context: Multiple teams, multiple clients, and a steady stream of small disagreements at handoff: which spacing value, which grey, which radius. Each one was cheap on its own and expensive in aggregate.
challenge: Give designers and developers a shared vocabulary that survives theming, client brands and new products — without a governance process nobody has time for.

approach.title: Primitive tier — the raw values
approach.body: The full palette, spacing scale, radii and type ramp, named for what they are, referenced by nothing but the tier above.

approach.title: Semantic tier — the intent
approach.body: surface, surface-raised, text-primary, text-muted, border-subtle, accent. Designers work here, which means a rebrand is a remap rather than a redraw.

approach.title: Component tier — the contract
approach.body: Per-component tokens that name the part being styled. This is the layer developers consume, so an interface change is a token change rather than a conversation.

approach.title: Rolled it out through the work, not a mandate
approach.body: Adopted project by project, with the token names appearing in handoff specs until using them was simply the path of least resistance.

outcomes: Adopted across product teams
Measurably less back-and-forth between design and development
Theming and client rebrands became a remap, not a redraw
New designers onboard against a documented vocabulary

title: EMAAR
subtitle: Concept to developer handoff, end to end
summary: Owned UX and UI from first concept through to developer handoff for a property brand where the browsing experience carries the weight of the product.
context: Property is a considered purchase researched over weeks. The interface has to hold detail — floor plans, availability, specifications — without turning the browse into work.
challenge: Design a browsing and enquiry experience that respects a long decision cycle and still moves people toward contact.

approach.title: Structured the catalogue around how people search
approach.body: People arrive with a location, a budget or a lifestyle in mind — rarely a project name. The architecture was built around those three entry points.

approach.title: Gave the imagery room to work
approach.body: In this category the photography is the product. Layout decisions consistently favoured the image over density.

approach.title: Made enquiry available without being intrusive
approach.body: Contact stays reachable at every depth of the journey rather than gating detail behind a form.

approach.title: Handed off with the questions answered
approach.body: Specs, states and edge cases resolved with PMs and BAs before development picked it up.

outcomes: A complete UX and UI system from concept to handoff
Browsing structured around real search behaviour
Fewer items returning for rework after handoff

title: Oneto11
subtitle: Fantasy sports, designed for the minute before kickoff
summary: UI for a fantasy sports platform, plus a library of 50+ reusable components adopted across teams.
context: Fantasy sports traffic arrives in a spike immediately before a match starts. Every interaction in the team-building flow is performed under time pressure.
challenge: Design an interface that stays readable and fast when a user is assembling a team with minutes on the clock.

approach.title: Optimised the team-building screen for speed
approach.body: Selection, credit budget and role constraints all had to be legible at once, without the screen becoming a wall of numbers.

approach.title: Made constraints visible before they are violated
approach.body: Budget and role limits show their state continuously, so a user learns the rules by playing rather than by hitting an error.

approach.title: Built a 50+ component library
approach.body: Reusable components covering the platform’s recurring patterns, which meant new screens were assembled rather than redrawn.

outcomes: A team-building flow that holds up under time pressure
50+ reusable components used across teams
Faster, more consistent delivery of new screens

title: Peet's Coffee
subtitle: A coffee app where every transition earns its place
summary: End-to-end UX and UI for the Peet’s Coffee app — complex ordering journeys turned into something a half-awake customer can complete without thinking about it.
context: Coffee ordering looks simple and is not. Customisation, store selection, rewards, scheduled pickup and payment all compete for the same few screens, and the customer is usually in a hurry.
challenge: Design an ordering experience where every screen, transition and interaction has a reason to be there — and none of them slow the customer down.

approach.title: Mapped the journey before drawing anything
approach.body: Every path through the app — first order, repeat order, rewards redemption, scheduled pickup — written out and compared, so the shared spine could be designed once.

approach.title: Made customisation feel like a choice, not a form
approach.body: Drink customisation is where most coffee apps become tedious. Defaults do the work, and the options open up only for the customer who wants them.

approach.title: Designed the transitions, not just the screens
approach.body: The movement between summary and detail is part of how the app explains itself. Each transition was specified rather than left to the build.

approach.title: Handed off with the reasoning attached
approach.body: Every screen came with the decision behind it, so the intent survived into development instead of being re-litigated.

outcomes: A complete ordering experience from first concept to developer handoff
Customisation that stays out of the way until it is wanted
Interaction and motion decisions specified rather than improvised

title: Scalable Super App
subtitle: One app, many products, a single navigational spine
summary: Designing a fintech super app: several distinct financial products living in one place without the app collapsing into a menu of menus.
context: Super apps fail in a predictable way. Each new product gets added as another tile, the home screen becomes a directory, and the thing that was supposed to simplify a customer’s financial life becomes another place to get lost.
challenge: Design a structure that can absorb new financial products over time without a redesign, and without the customer having to relearn where anything is.

approach.title: Designed the spine before the products
approach.body: One navigational structure that every product plugs into, defined first, so adding a product later is an insertion rather than a renegotiation.

approach.title: Made the home screen answer a question
approach.body: Not "what can this app do" but "what is the state of my money right now". Products surface when they are relevant rather than sitting in a permanent grid.

approach.title: Built the shared component vocabulary
approach.body: Balance, transaction, product card, action sheet — defined once, reused everywhere, so a customer moving between products stays on familiar ground.

approach.title: Pressure-tested with products that did not exist yet
approach.body: The structure was checked against hypothetical future products, on the assumption that whatever ships first will not be the last thing added.

outcomes: A navigational structure that absorbs new products without redesign
A shared component vocabulary across financial products
A home screen organised around the customer’s position, not the product catalogue

title: Jimmy John's Kiosk
subtitle: Ordering at arm’s length, under a queue
summary: A self-service ordering kiosk designed for the two constraints a phone never has: you are standing up, and there is a queue behind you.
context: Kiosk ordering is not mobile ordering on a bigger screen. The customer is standing, reading from a distance, using a finger on glass they have never touched before, and aware of the people waiting behind them.
challenge: Design an ordering flow that a first-time user can complete quickly and confidently, at kiosk distance, without help from staff.

approach.title: Sized everything for standing distance
approach.body: Type scale, target sizes and contrast set for a screen read at arm’s length rather than held in the hand.

approach.title: Kept the number of decisions visibly finite
approach.body: A customer under queue pressure needs to see how much is left. Progress stays visible so the flow never feels open-ended.

approach.title: Made every step reversible
approach.body: Undo and back are always available and always in the same place, so a mistake costs a tap rather than a restart.

approach.title: Designed for the idle state too
approach.body: The attract screen, the timeout, the reset between customers — the states that decide whether the next person walks up at all.

outcomes: A flow a first-time customer can finish without staff help
Legibility and target sizes tuned for kiosk distance
Complete state coverage, including attract, timeout and reset
